items.title: Microorganism groups and observable evidence
items.student: Classify each source-approved example as a fungus, bacterium or virus. For each, distinguish what the image/model shows from what it cannot show, and identify one way it can affect people.
items.teacher: Use teacher-previewed sources and age-appropriate examples. Fungi, bacteria and viruses are distinct groups; a picture alone does not establish that an organism causes a particular infection. Avoid diagnosing people or implying all members of a group are harmful.

items.title: Helpful and harmful effects
items.student: Sort supplied examples into useful, harmful or context-dependent effects of microorganisms on people. Explain one economic benefit and one cost, naming the evidence needed for each claim.
items.teacher: Examples may include food fermentation, decomposition and spoilage or infection. Not all microorganisms are pathogens; preserve distinctions between economic examples and measured local impacts.

items.title: Transmission route matching
items.student: For four teacher-approved fictional scenarios, match the stated infection and contact history to a possible transmission route (direct contact, respiratory particles, contaminated food/water or a vector). Identify one uncertainty in each scenario.
items.teacher: Use medically accurate, reviewed examples; routes are organism-specific. A scenario does not establish diagnosis or causation. Do not ask learners to disclose personal illness or contacts.

items.title: Infection categories and evidence
items.student: Sort reviewed examples of fungal, bacterial and viral infections. For each example, state the source that supports the category and one prevention or control measure that matches its transmission route.
items.teacher: Use reliable public-health or curriculum sources selected by the teacher. Do not present antibiotics as treatment for viral infections; no learner diagnosis or treatment recommendation.

items.title: Match prevention to transmission
items.student: Evaluate a set of fictional prevention plans. Match handwashing, safe food/water handling, ventilation or avoiding shared contaminated items to the stated route; reject measures that do not address the route and explain why.
items.teacher: Measures are examples, not a complete medical protocol. Emphasise route-specific prevention, access and reputable guidance; no stigma or blame.

items.title: Control and prevention are related
items.student: Compare a prevention action before exposure with a control action after an identified risk. Explain how sanitation, safe handling, isolation under professional guidance or vaccination where applicable can reduce risk, and name a limit of each example.
items.teacher: Keep vaccination/general health information aligned to current local public-health sources; do not give personal medical advice or imply one measure prevents every infection.

items.title: Economic roles of microorganisms
items.student: Use supplied evidence cards to explain two ways microorganisms contribute to economic activity and one way microbial growth can cause loss. Separate a general example from a measured local claim.
items.teacher: Possible examples include fermentation, decomposition, food spoilage and infection-related costs. Do not invent local prices or economic measurements.

items.title: Food preservation choices
items.student: Compare drying, cooling, heating, salting, sugaring and fermentation using a provided information table. Recommend one method for a fictional food and explain the conditions, benefits and limitations using the supplied evidence.
items.teacher: Do not treat a classroom comparison as proof that food is safe. No tasting, consumption or home-preservation instruction; use teacher-reviewed food-safety sources.

items.title: Plan a safe mould-growth investigation
items.student: Review a teacher-prepared plan for observing mould growth on food substrates. Identify the comparison, observation schedule, records and safety controls. Use supplied dated images/data if no approved sealed observation is available; state clearly whether any growth was actually observed.
items.teacher: Any sample must be prepared and sealed by the teacher under school approval, allergy-aware material choice and a disposal plan. Learners do not open, touch, smell, incubate at body temperature or take samples home. A supplied record is not student performance evidence.

items.title: Read observation records without overclaiming
items.student: Compare supplied dated observations from two sealed food-substrate samples. Describe the visible change, identify what was held constant or changed, and explain why the observations do not identify the microorganism or prove a general rule.
items.teacher: Label all records as supplied unless genuinely observed. No organism identification from appearance alone and no opening of containers. Discuss uncontrolled conditions and replicate limits.

items.title: Review a community food-preservation message
items.student: Draft a short, evidence-based food-preservation message for a fictional community audience. Check that it states a practical benefit and limitation, uses a reliable source and avoids claiming that one method prevents all spoilage or infection.
items.teacher: A learner draft is not a community sensitisation event. Actual distribution or presentation requires school/community approval and a reviewed message.

items.title: Integrated infection and daily-life case
items.student: For a fictional food-service case, identify the microorganism group and stated infection category, trace the supported transmission route, recommend route-matched prevention/control and food-preservation actions, and explain one economic effect and one evidence limit.
items.teacher: All case facts are fictional/supplied. Mark each inference against the stated evidence; do not diagnose a real person or claim that learners performed an investigation or community activity.
